hints: Sort the four compounds first by functional group, think why any $COOH$ acid is far stronger than an alcohol $OH$ even before looking at substituents.
For the three carboxylic acids, focus on what is attached to the alpha carbon and how it pulls or pushes electrons toward the $O-H$ bond.
Recall how an electron withdrawing group affects the stability of the carboxylate anion $RCOO^-$ formed after losing $H^+$.
Compare Cl and Br by electronegativity to decide which $XCH_2COOH$ is stronger, and think about the alkyl group in $CH_3COOH$ versus $H$ in the substituted acids.
walkthrough:
Separate acids from alcohols**
Picture what happens when each loses $H^+$. A carboxylic acid gives $RCOO^-$ where the negative charge is spread over two oxygens by resonance. An alcohol gives $RO^-$ with the charge stuck on one oxygen. That delocalisation makes every carboxylic acid here far stronger than ethanol, so $CH_3CH_2OH$ is clearly least acidic.

Think in terms of the anion left behind**
Acid strength is really about how comfortable the molecule is losing $H^+$. If the anion formed is stable, the acid is strong. Anything that pulls electron density away from the $O-H$ helps spread the negative charge and weakens the $O-H$ bond. We call this an electron withdrawing, negative inductive effect. Anything that pushes electrons toward the $O-H$ does the opposite.

Rank the three carboxylic acids**
$CH_3COOH$ has an electron donating $CH_3$ group pushing electrons toward $COO^-$, destabilising it, so it is the weakest of the three acids. $BrCH_2COOH$ and $ClCH_2COOH$ have electronegative halogens pulling electrons away, stabilising $XCH_2COO^-$. Because Cl is more electronegative than Br, its withdrawing power is greater, so $ClCH_2COOH$ stabilises the anion most and is the strongest acid.

Add the carbonyl effect**
Remember also that the $C=O$ part of every $COOH$ group is itself electron withdrawing. That is part of why $CH_3COOH$ is still far stronger than $CH_3CH_2OH$, where the ethyl group is electron donating with no withdrawing $C=O$ to help. Put together: $ClCH_2COOH$ (strongest withdrawing) > $BrCH_2COOH$ > $CH_3COOH$ > $CH_3CH_2OH$ (donating, no $C=O$).

Final answer: most acidic $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH}$ > $\text{BrCH}_2\text{COOH}$ > $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ > $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ least acidic.
Electron withdrawing groups exert a negative inductive effect, weakening the $O-H$ bond and stabilising the anion formed. Electron donating alkyl groups exert a positive inductive effect, strengthening the $O-H$ bond and destabilising the anion.
Cl is more electronegative and more electron withdrawing than Br. The $C=O$ in $COOH$ is electron withdrawing. Alkyl / ethyl groups in $CH_3COOH$ and $CH_3CH_2OH$ are electron donating.

hints: Recall what hot alkaline $KMnO_4$ does to an alkyl side chain on a benzene ring, however long the chain is.
Think what happens when ethanedioic acid $(COOH)_2$, already highly oxidised, is heated with strong acidified $KMnO_4$.
walkthrough:
Oxidise the methyl side chain completely**
With hot alkaline $KMnO_4$, the benzene ring itself survives but the whole alkyl side chain is chopped back to the benzylic carbon and oxidised up to $COOH$. So $C_6H_5CH_3$ gives $C_6H_5COOH$, benzoic acid, as the only carbon containing product. The ring is not broken.

Oxidise ethanedioic acid to the top oxidation state**
Ethanedioic acid is $HOOC-COOH$. Carbon is already at +3. Hot acidified $MnO_4^-$ is a very powerful oxidiser and cleaves the $C-C$ bond, pushing each carbon to +4 in $CO_2$. So:
$$ (COOH)_2 \xrightarrow{\text{hot acidified } KMnO_4} 2CO_2 + 2H^+ + 2e^- \text{ (overall) } $$
The carbon product is simply $CO_2$.

Final answer: methylbenzene $\rightarrow$ benzoic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$ (benzene ring bonded to $COOH$).
ethanedioic acid $\rightarrow$ $\text{CO}_2$.

hints: Identify the two reacting groups, $COOH$ from ethanedioic acid and $NH_2$ from the diamine, and recall what new link plus small molecule they form.
Think how to join one $HOOC-COOH$ unit to one $-HN-C_6H_4-NH-$ unit with continuation bonds at each end to show the polymer chain continues.
walkthrough:
Spot the condensation**
You have a diacid $HOOC-COOH$ and a diamine $H_2N-C_6H_4-NH_2$. Each $COOH + H_2N-$ pair forms an amide $CONH$ plus $H_2O$. Because each monomer has two functional groups, the chain can grow both ways.

Build the repeat unit**
Take one whole diacid residue $-CO-CO-$ and one whole diamine residue $-NH-C_6H_4-NH-$ and join them:
$$ -C(=O)-C(=O)-NH-C_6H_4-NH- $$
Show both $C=O$ bonds displayed, the $N$ bonded to the benzene and to the carbonyl $C$, the benzene para substituted, and put continuation bonds at the left $C$ and right $N$ to show it repeats. That is polyamide X.

Final answer: Repeat unit: $-[C(=O)-C(=O)-NH-C_6H_4-NH]-$ with continuation bonds through the outer C and N atoms.
Amide groups shown displayed as $-C(=O)-NH-$, benzene as para-disubstituted $C_6H_4$, i.e. $-[CO-CO-NH-C_6H_4-NH]-$.

hints: Count how many $[H]$ are needed to turn one $NO_2$ into $NH_2$ (oxygen must end up as water) and then double it for the dinitro compound.
walkthrough:
Balance nitro to amine reduction**
Each $NO_2 \rightarrow NH_2$ needs $6[H]$ to strip the two oxygens as $2H_2O$ and add two hydrogens to nitrogen. You have two nitro groups in 1,4-dinitrobenzene, so double everything:
$$ O_2N-C_6H_4-NO_2 + 12[H] \rightarrow H_2N-C_6H_4-NH_2 + 4H_2O $$
Keep the para substitution pattern unchanged.

hints: In step 1 both $NH_2$ groups of benzene-1,4-diamine are diazotised, think what $N$-containing cation replaces each $NH_2$ and what anion balances it.
In step 2 each diazonium group couples to one phenol molecule in alkaline solution, think where on phenol coupling occurs and how many phenols add to the central ring.
walkthrough:
Form the double diazonium salt V**
Benzene-1,4-diamine has two $NH_2$ groups, so diazotisation happens twice. Each $-NH_2$ becomes $-N^+ \equiv N$ with a $Cl^-$ counter ion:
$$ H_2N-C_6H_4-NH_2 \rightarrow Cl^-\; ^+N \equiv N-C_6H_4-N^+ \equiv N\; Cl^- $$
Keep the para relationship on the central ring. Formula $C_6H_4N_4Cl_2$ fits two $N_2^+$ plus two $Cl^-$.

Couple twice to make bis-azo dye W**
In NaOH(aq), phenol exists as phenoxide and couples to each diazonium $N$. One V reacts with two phenols, giving a central $C_6H_4$ with an $-N=N-$ link on each side to a $C_6H_4OH$ ring:
$$ HO-C_6H_4-N=N-C_6H_4-N=N-C_6H_4-OH $$
Each coupling is para to the $OH$ (ortho if para blocked, but here para is free), giving $C_{18}H_{14}N_4O_2$. This extended conjugated azo system is compound W.

Final answer: V: para $\text{Cl}^-\;^+\text{N}\equiv\text{N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{N}^+\equiv\text{N}\;\text{Cl}^-$, benzene-1,4-bis(diazonium) dichloride.
W: $\text{HO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{N=N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{N=N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{OH}$, central para $C_6H_4$ linked by two $N=N$ to two para $HO-C_6H_4$ groups.

hints: Recall the in situ source of nitrous acid $HNO_2$ for diazotisation and the critical low temperature needed to keep the diazonium ion stable.
walkthrough:
Choose diazotisation conditions**
Diazotisation needs nitrous acid made in situ from $NaNO_2$ plus excess HCl. The $^+N \equiv N$ ion decomposes easily to $N_2$ if warm, so keep the mixture ice cold, below $10^{\circ}C$, typically 0 to $5^{\circ}C$. No heating, no alkaline conditions here.
Final answer: Step 1: $\text{NaNO}_2$ + HCl (i.e. $\text{HNO}_2$ + HCl) with temperature $\leqslant 10^{\circ}\text{C}$ (0 to 5 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ in ice bath).
